item.title: Session Log
item.description: The PoliCICS working group maintains an active calendar of regular sessions, traditionally held on Thursdays at 11:30 AM. These instances constitute a fundamental space for discussing research progress, piloting experimental designs, and presenting work by both our researchers and national and international guests. Below you can see the record of the sessions held during the 2025 academic cycle, from most recent to oldest. Date Presenter Title Abstract December 4 Constanza Pino (CICS) Interventions for Food Consumption in Adult Women Through Embodiment Mechanisms In this project, food choice in adult women will be explored under the cognitive embodiment framework.

item.title: Communicating Sustainability: How Ecological Information and Moral Messages Shape Extraction Decisions in Common-Pool Resources
item.description: Common-pool resources face the challenge of reconciling individual extraction with resource sustainability. Their management requires individuals to understand the ecological dynamics of the resource and consider the collective and future consequences of their decisions. However, information about resource conditions and regeneration does not necessarily guarantee sustainable decisions. It is therefore important to assess whether providing explicit and updated information about the Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY), together with different communication mechanisms, can guide individual decisions.

item.title: Financial News Sentiment and Commodity Market Dynamics
item.description: Commodity markets respond to supply and demand conditions, expectations and information flows that change continuously. Beyond reporting relevant facts, financial news can reflect perceptions of risks, opportunities and future scenarios. This project seeks to study the relationship between the sentiment expressed in that news and the evolution of returns and volatility in these markets. The project is carried out by Juan Illanes (Ph.D. student, Universidad del Desarrollo), with advisors Juan Pablo Couyoumdjian (School of Government, Universidad del Desarrollo; CICS member) and María Paz Raveau (Faro UDD; CICS member).

item.title: How Parliaments Polarize: Legislative Replacement and Adaptation in Chile
item.description: The growing polarization of political elites is usually interpreted as the result of a progressive radicalization of their members. However, a parliament can also become more polarized without its members substantially changing their positions, simply because incoming legislators are more extreme than those they replace. Distinguishing between these two mechanisms is key to understanding how political representation changes over time. The project is carried out by Jorge Fábrega. Data and methodology The project analyzes roll-call votes in Chile’s Chamber of Deputies over six legislative periods, from 2002 to 2026.

item.title: Identity, Experience, and Persistent Expectations in Social Dilemmas: An Experimental Approach
item.description: This research addresses social dilemmas, which are situations where individual incentives are misaligned with collective welfare. The central problem examines how social identity influences empirical belief formation and its persistence over time. We argue that identity serves as a heuristic that individuals use to form expectations about others’ behavior under uncertainty. We hypothesize that cooperation is driven by these identity-based beliefs, and the persistence—or “stickiness”—of these expectations is fundamentally a function of prior real-world intergroup experience.

item.title: Network Disadoption: exposure to disadoption as an indicator of social contagion
item.description: Research on the diffusion of innovations has focused on adoption: moving from not using to using a practice. Its natural counterpart, disadoption (stopping its use), has received far less attention, even though it is a substantively different process. This project asks whether abandoning a behavior also spreads through the network, and how to measure that influence. The work is carried out by Aníbal Olivera in collaboration with Thomas W. Valente and the team at the Center for Applied Network Analysis (USC).

item.title: Networks Decide for Us: network structure as a causal force in diffusion
item.description: The diffusion of collective behaviors is usually modeled as the outcome of individual decisions or as a contagion process. This project starts from a different question: if we hold each person’s propensities fixed, does diffusion change just because the shape of the network changes? The argument is that networks “decide for us”: relational structure, shaped by homophily, enables or constrains social change beyond the sum of individual preferences. The project is carried out by Aníbal Olivera and Jorge Fábrega (CICS, UDD) together with Thomas W.

item.title: Political Networks: collaboration in the Constitutional Convention (2021–2022)
item.description: Chile’s Constitutional Convention (2021–2022) is a rare natural experiment for studying how political collaboration organizes from scratch: a majority of delegates with no prior political experience, a body that dissolved upon delivering its draft, and procedural rules written by its own members. Two of those rules structure the study. Each constitutional initiative required between 8 and 16 signatures, so signing amounted to forming a visible, dated coalition. In addition, each provision needed two thirds of the plenary (103 of 154 votes) to pass.

item.title: New publication in Applied Network Science: Same score, different network
item.description: PoliCICS researchers Jorge Fábrega and Aníbal Olivera published the article “Same score, different network: configuration-level heterogeneity in composite risk measures” in Applied Network Science. The work proposes a network-based framework for examining cases that share the same risk score but may differ in how their factors are organized. Using 17,272 administrative assessments from a criminological instrument applied by Chile’s prison service (Gendarmería de Chile), the authors show that identical scores can correspond to distinct, recurrent network architectures, and that some patterns of item co-presence are associated with recidivism.

item.title: Launch of Deputies Dataset 2002-2026
item.description: The PoliCICS laboratory is pleased to announce the launch of the Deputies Dataset 2002-2026, a new public resource developed by researcher Jorge Fábrega. This dataset provides systematic estimates of the ideological positions of all members of the Chilean Chamber of Deputies across six consecutive legislative periods. The estimates are based exclusively on roll-call votes related to bill proposals debated and voted on in plenary sessions, offering a robust tool for legislative analysis.
